interactions.label: Depth Z
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates the 1/Z scaling of optical flow: as the 3D point moves further away, the magnitude of its projected 2D velocity ṗ decreases rapidly.

interactions.label: 3D Velocity Angle (deg)
interactions.teaches: Varies the ratio of lateral velocity (dX) to velocity in depth (dZ), modifying the perspective projection components to show how 3D direction shapes 2D optical flow.

interactions.label: Reposition P
interactions.teaches: Allows directly shifting the 3D point's XY position to observe how its off-axis coordinates (x, y) dynamically scale the radial component of 2D velocity via -dZ*x/Z.

demo_steps.title: 3D Motion Projection
demo_steps.narration: A 3D point P moves with velocity Ṗ. Its perspective projection p onto the image plane moves with 2D velocity ṗ. Observe the primary ray (solid) and the future ray (dashed) passing through the tips of their respective velocity vectors.

demo_steps.title: Pure Lateral Motion
demo_steps.narration: With 3D velocity aligned parallel to the image plane (velocity angle = 90°), the term dZ becomes zero. The 2D velocity ṗ is simply scaled by f/Z: vx = f*dX/Z and vy = f*dY/Z. The 2D flow perfectly matches the 3D direction.

demo_steps.title: Pure Depth Motion
demo_steps.narration: When motion is purely along the depth axis (velocity angle = 180°), lateral 3D motion is zero (dX=dY=0). The resulting 2D flow is purely radial, pointing directly toward the center: vx = -dZ*x/Z. This explains why looming objects create expanding flow fields.

demo_steps.title: Depth Scale Suppression
demo_steps.narration: Push the point far away to Z = 12. Although the physical 3D velocity vector Ṗ remains identical, notice how both the projected point p shifts inward and the projected flow vector ṗ dramatically shrinks, illustrating the strong damping effect of distance.

plan.camera_suggestion: Elevated perspective looking down-right along the optical axis, showcasing the geometry from origin to point P.
plan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant baseline is the optical axis running from the origin O, through the center of the image plane, to the point P. In the source image, this line recedes diagonally into the background toward the upper-right. (2) This receding baseline implies a camera azimuth angle of around 40 degrees, preventing the origin, image plane, and point P from overlapping. (3) The vertical offset of the projected point relative to the origin shows a clear elevation angle of approximately 15 degrees, presenting a clean 3D look.

camera_view.view_notes: Positioned to perfectly align with the textbook figure silhouette: camera origin O is at the bottom-left, the translucent image plane is mid-ground, and the point P is situated in the upper-right background.

phase2Evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several high-quality interactions: (1) A 'Depth Z' slider that dynamically scales the depth coordinate of point P and recalculates the perspective projection and 2D/3D velocity vectors; (2) A 'Motion Direction' slider that rotates the 3D velocity vector and updates the corresponding perspective projection derivative; (3) A guided step-through demo with 'Prev' and 'Next' buttons that animate the parameters between key physical scenarios; (4) Clickable 3D scene elements (camera center O, image plane, projection ray, points, and velocity vectors) which trigger descriptive educational overlays and/or transition the demo to relevant states. While the planned direct-drag interaction for point P was omitted, the interactive sliders, step-by-step navigation, and clickable 3D annotations provide an exceptionally rich, functional, and pedagogically useful experience.
phase2Evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concept: 3D motion projection and the perspective relationship between 3D velocity Ṗ and 2D optical flow ṗ. User-visible claims: (1) Step 2 claims 'Mostly Lateral Motion' where 'Ẋ and Ẏ terms dominate', and Step 3 claims 'Motion in Depth' where 'Ż component changes depth'. In reality, the code rotates the velocity vector Ṗ around the ray axis (O-P line) using `applyAxisAngle(rayAxis, delta)`. Rotating around the ray axis keeps the angle with the ray constant, meaning the ratio of lateral velocity to depth velocity remains constant; it only rotates the clock-angle of the lateral motion rather than actually transitioning from lateral to depth motion. While the math for calculating the resulting ṗ is conceptually correct, the physical 3D vector does not align as claimed by the steps (i.e. it does not become purely lateral or purely depth-based).
phase2Evaluation.concept_accuracy_improvement: Modify the 3D velocity calculation so that the 'Motion Direction' slider actually interpolates the 3D velocity vector Ṗ between being parallel to the image plane (pure lateral, Ż = 0) and parallel to the optical axis (pure depth, Ẋ = Ẏ = 0), matching the textual descriptions of the steps.
phase2Evaluation.notes: While the interactivity and visual alignment of the figure are excellent, the 3D physics contains a conceptual flaw: rotating the velocity vector around the projection ray keeps the ratio of lateral-to-depth motion constant. This directly contradicts the guided steps, which describe transitions between lateral motion and motion in depth.
action_items: Modify the calculation of vel3D in computeDynamicGeometry so that the 'Motion Direction' slider changes the angle of Ṗ relative to the projection ray, interpolating between pure lateral motion (perpendicular to the ray, Z-dot = 0) and pure depth motion (along the ray, X-dot = Y-dot = 0).

Update the 3D velocity vector (Ṗ) and 2D projected velocity vector (ṗ) calculations so that the arrows physically align with the descriptions in step 2 ('Mostly Lateral Motion') and step 3 ('Motion in Depth').

plan.contextChunk:
## Introduction

As objects move in the world, or as the camera moves, the projection of
the dynamic scene into the two-dimensional (2D) camera plane produces a
sequence of temporally varying pixel brightness. Before diving into how
to estimate motion from pixels, it is useful to understand the image
formation process. Studying how three-dimensional (3D) motion projects
into the camera will allow us to understand what the difference is
between a moving camera or a moving object and what types of constraints
one might be able to use to estimate motion.

## 3D Motion and Its 2D Projection {#d-motion-and-its-2d-projection}

A 3D point will follow a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$,
in camera coordinates (@fig-optical_flow_basic_motion_point). As the
point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of
$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The
projection of this point into the image plane location is
$\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D
instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$,
where all the derivatives are done with respect to time, $t$.

![A 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, moving in the world projects a 2D moving point, $\mathbf{p}$, into the camera plane.](figures/optical_flow/basic_motion_point.png){width="50%" #fig-optical_flow_basic_motion_point}

Using the equations of perspective projection $x=f X/Z$ and $y=f Y/Z$
(assuming that the camera is at the origin of the world-coordinate
system), we can derive the equations of how the instantaneous velocity
in the camera plane relates to the point motion in 3D world coordinates:
$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\
\dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} 
\end{aligned}$$ The second expression is obtained by using $x=f \, X/Z$
and $y=f \, Y/Z$, which removes the dependency on the world coordinates
$X$ and $Y$. Note that $f$ is the focal length. In many derivations, the
notation is simplified by setting the focal length $f=1$. Here we will
keep it to make explicit which factors depend on the camera parameters
and which ones do not. We can write the last two equations in matrix
form as:

interactions.teaches: Demonstrates that as the 3D point moves further away (larger Z), the projected 2D velocity shrinking rapidly due to the 1/Z scaling factor.

interactions.label: Motion Direction
interactions.teaches: Rotates the 3D velocity vector to show how lateral motion vs. motion along the optical axis affects the 2D projected velocity vector differently.

demo_steps.title: 3D Motion Projection
demo_steps.narration: A 3D point P moves through space with instantaneous velocity vector Ṗ. Its perspective projection onto the image plane is point p, which moves with 2D velocity vector ṗ. The green dashed line shows where the ray will point at the next instant.

demo_steps.title: Pure Lateral Motion
demo_steps.narration: When the 3D velocity is purely lateral (parallel to the image plane), the projected 2D velocity ṗ aligns perfectly with the direction of Ṗ, scaled simply by f/Z. The mapping is linear and direct.

demo_steps.title: Motion in Depth
demo_steps.narration: When the point moves along the optical axis (towards/away from the camera), it produces a radial projected velocity ṗ that points directly towards or away from the center, scaled by -Ẑ/Z. Even with no lateral 3D motion, we observe 2D motion!

demo_steps.title: The Scaling Effect of Distance
demo_steps.narration: Move the 3D point twice as far away (Z=12). Notice how the projected 2D velocity vector ṗ shrinks dramatically, even though the physical 3D velocity vector Ṗ remains exactly the same size. This illustrates the inverse-depth scaling of optical flow.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Slightly elevated perspective looking from behind and to the left of the camera center, showing the image plane intersecting the projection rays clearly.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant baseline is the optical axis running from the origin O, through the center of the image plane, to the point P. In the source image, this axis recedes into the page and to the right. (2) This receding baseline implies a camera azimuth angle of around 45 to 55 degrees off-axis to clearly separate O, the image plane, and P without them overlapping. (3) The tilt of the image plane and the vertical separation of the rays suggest an elevation angle of 15 to 20 degrees.

camera_view.view_notes: Positioned to match the exact perspective of the textbook figure, where the camera origin O is on the far left, the image plane is tilted in the foreground, and point P is in the far right background.

inline_constraints.framing: match the source crop and whitespace

The green line from O to P must render with a solid segment up to the image plane, then a slightly dimmer segment to P. The future-ray dashed line connects O to the tip of the velocity vector P + Ṗ, intersecting the image plane exactly at p + ṗ to geometrically prove the projection equations.

\dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\

\end{aligned}$$ The second expression is obtained by using $x=f \, X/Z$
and $y=f \, Y/Z$, which removes the dependency on the world coordinates
$X$ and $Y$. Note that $f$ is the focal length. In many derivations, the
notation is simplified by setting the focal length $f=1$. Here we will

demo_steps.title: Pure Lateral Motion

demo_steps.title: Pure Depth Motion
demo_steps.narration: When motion is purely along the depth axis (velocity angle = 180°), lateral 3D motion is zero (dX=dY=0). The resulting 2D flow is purely radial, pointing directly toward the center: vx = -dZ*x/Z. This explains why looming objects create expanding flow fields.

demo_steps.narration: Push the point far away to Z = 12. Although the physical 3D velocity vector Ṗ remains identical, notice how both the projected point p shifts inward and the projected flow vector ṗ dramatically shrinks, illustrating the strong damping effect of distance.

evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several high-quality interactions: (1) A 'Depth Z' slider that dynamically scales the depth coordinate of point P and recalculates the perspective projection and 2D/3D velocity vectors; (2) A 'Motion Direction' slider that rotates the 3D velocity vector and updates the corresponding perspective projection derivative; (3) A guided step-through demo with 'Prev' and 'Next' buttons that animate the parameters between key physical scenarios; (4) Clickable 3D scene elements (camera center O, image plane, projection ray, points, and velocity vectors) which trigger descriptive educational overlays and/or transition the demo to relevant states. While the planned direct-drag interaction for point P was omitted, the interactive sliders, step-by-step navigation, and clickable 3D annotations provide an exceptionally rich, functional, and pedagogically useful experience.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concept: 3D motion projection and the perspective relationship between 3D velocity Ṗ and 2D optical flow ṗ. User-visible claims: (1) Step 2 claims 'Mostly Lateral Motion' where 'Ẋ and Ẏ terms dominate', and Step 3 claims 'Motion in Depth' where 'Ż component changes depth'. In reality, the code rotates the velocity vector Ṗ around the ray axis (O-P line) using `applyAxisAngle(rayAxis, delta)`. Rotating around the ray axis keeps the angle with the ray constant, meaning the ratio of lateral velocity to depth velocity remains constant; it only rotates the clock-angle of the lateral motion rather than actually transitioning from lateral to depth motion. While the math for calculating the resulting ṗ is conceptually correct, the physical 3D vector does not align as claimed by the steps (i.e. it does not become purely lateral or purely depth-based).
evaluation.concept_accuracy_improvement: Modify the 3D velocity calculation so that the 'Motion Direction' slider actually interpolates the 3D velocity vector Ṗ between being parallel to the image plane (pure lateral, Ż = 0) and parallel to the optical axis (pure depth, Ẋ = Ẏ = 0), matching the textual descriptions of the steps.
evaluation.notes: While the interactivity and visual alignment of the figure are excellent, the 3D physics contains a conceptual flaw: rotating the velocity vector around the projection ray keeps the ratio of lateral-to-depth motion constant. This directly contradicts the guided steps, which describe transitions between lateral motion and motion in depth.
